structure.title: Module 3: Knowledge Base Engine
structure.prefix_summary: This partial document describes Module 3: Knowledge Base Engine, which serves as the intelligence layer of a platform. The module is responsible for ingesting, processing, classifying, indexing, and retrieving knowledge used by agents for generating recommendations, discovery questions, emails, and competitive positioning. The architecture consists of two parallel systems: (1) Azure Foundry IQ, a managed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) service that handles unstructured content processing (document parsing, chunking, vectorization, and hybrid retrieval), and (2) a custom Knowledge Base (KB) layer that manages structured knowledge (product relationship graphs, content classification, competitor profiles, customer patterns, playbooks), tenant lifecycle, caching, and context assembly. The document emphasizes a critical architectural distinction: Foundry IQ provides foundational unstructured data processing capabilities, while the custom KB layer adds proprietary features and structured intelligence, building on top of Foundry IQ rather than replacing it.

nodes.title: 3.1 Ingestion Layer
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.1 Ingestion Layer

The ingestion layer is a fan-out pipeline. A single file upload triggers multiple parallel downstream processes: raw storage, Foundry IQ indexing, content classification with intelligence extraction, and metadata cataloging. It is not a simple file upload.

nodes.title: 3.1.1 Ingestion Flow — Step by Step
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the step-by-step ingestion flow for uploading documents into a tenant-scoped knowledge base system. It covers: (1) uploading files to a tenant-isolated blob storage structure, ensuring tenant data separation; (2) deduplication and versioning by checking a PostgreSQL catalog to prevent duplicates and manage file versions; (3) recording document metadata in the KB catalog as the authoritative source of document state; (4) triggering an asynchronous content classification job to extract structured information from the document; and (5) leveraging Foundry IQ’s managed auto-indexing pipeline, which detects new files, parses, chunks, vectorizes, and indexes them on a scheduled or on-demand basis. The document emphasizes automation, data integrity, and separation of responsibilities in the ingestion process.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Ingestion Caveats
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines key caveats in the data ingestion process for a multi-tenant system. It highlights: (1) multi-destination routing, where a single uploaded document is simultaneously processed and routed to multiple destinations for storage, indexing, analysis, and metadata extraction; (2) deduplication and versioning, ensuring that updates to existing data are correctly identified, versioned, and trigger necessary downstream analyses and re-indexing; and (3) tenant-scoped isolation, emphasizing strict separation of data and metadata by tenant to prevent cross-tenant data leaks, using both storage and database-level isolation mechanisms.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Supported File Types and Parsing Strategy
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the supported file types and the parsing strategy for each within the system. It presents a table detailing how different file formats (CSV/Excel, PDF, Word, Markdown, PowerPoint, plain text, and transaction CSV) are processed, specifying the parser used, the data destination, and special handling notes. The main decision is to use Foundry IQ (leveraging Azure Content Understanding) for all unstructured document types, benefiting from its layout-aware enrichment and semantic indexing capabilities. Custom parsers are reserved for structured data (product catalogs and transaction histories in CSV/Excel), where precise row-level control is required. The rationale for this approach is to avoid the significant engineering effort and likely lower quality of building a custom multi-format parser, instead relying on Microsoft's managed service for superior results.

nodes.title: 3.2.1 Content Classifier — Cross-KB Intelligence Extraction
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the Content Classifier module for cross-KB intelligence extraction. It explains how uploaded documents are analyzed by a large language model (LLM) to extract structured intelligence, which is then used to update multiple downstream knowledge bases, such as semantic search indexes, product relationship graphs, competitor profiles, customer success patterns, and metadata catalogs. The classifier categorizes documents into types like product catalogs, case studies, sales playbooks, competitor intelligence, pricing sheets, technical specs, training materials, and general documents, extracting relevant information for each. It supports multi-category classification and outputs structured JSON with detailed intelligence fields (e.g., products mentioned, relationships, competitors, customer info, metrics). The document also details the decision to use a cost-effective LLM variant (Gpt-4.1-mini) for classification and extraction, citing scalability and quality considerations.

nodes.title: 3.2.2 Intelligence Routing — Fan-Out From Classifier
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Intelligence Routing — Fan-Out From Classifier" process, detailing how extracted intelligence from documents is routed to various data stores after classification. It covers four main routing targets: (1) updating the product graph by adding or strengthening edges based on detected product relationships, (2) upserting competitor profiles with new or enriched data, (3) aggregating customer outcome data into customer patterns for industry/segment/product combinations, and (4) updating knowledge base catalog metadata with classification results and status. Each routing operation is independent and can fail without impacting the others.

nodes.title: 3.2.3 Chunking Strategy
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the chunking strategy for handling unstructured and structured content. It describes how Foundry IQ is used to automatically chunk unstructured text documents by semantic boundaries, with configurable chunk sizes and overlapping windows for context preservation. For layout-aware documents processed with Azure Content Understanding, tables are kept intact, headers and section titles are preserved as metadata, and figures receive alt-text descriptions. Each chunk is vectorized using Azure OpenAI embeddings for hybrid retrieval. The only custom chunking occurs for structured product catalog data, where each product is indexed as a separate document with fielded attributes. The decision is to delegate all unstructured chunking to Foundry IQ, reserving custom chunking solely for structured product catalog entries, due to the complexity and engineering effort required for high-quality chunking pipelines.

nodes.title: 3.3 KB Core — Knowledge Stores
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.3 KB Core — Knowledge Stores

| Two Types of Stores Per Tenant Each tenant has: (1) ONE Foundry IQ Knowledge Base — the unified semantic search layer containing all unstructured content (product descriptions, case studies, playbooks, competitor sheets, technical specs). Not separated into multiple indexes per content type — it is one KB with multiple knowledge sources. (2) FIVE PostgreSQL structured stores — holding queryable structured data: products table, product_relationships (graph), competitor_profiles, customer_patterns, playbook_index, plus the kb_documents catalog. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 3.3.1 Foundry IQ Knowledge Base Architecture
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the architecture of the Foundry IQ Knowledge Base (KB), focusing on its per-tenant structure. Each tenant has a dedicated KB containing multiple knowledge sources, such as product descriptions, case studies, sales playbooks, competitor intelligence, and technical specifications, all stored in tenant-specific blobs. The system uses a GPT-4.1 LLM for query planning, enabling intelligent source selection based on the nature of the query. Retrieval reasoning effort is configurable, with three levels: low (simple keyword and vector search), medium (LLM-driven subquery decomposition and semantic reranking), and high (multi-step reasoning with iterative planning across sources). The document outlines how different agent queries trigger different retrieval strategies and details the cost and use cases for each reasoning level.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Metadata Model Per KB Type
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the structured metadata models maintained in PostgreSQL for different knowledge base (KB) types beyond what is indexed by Foundry IQ. It details the specific metadata fields and their intended uses for five KB types: Product Catalog (e.g., SKU, category, features, vendor, used for lookups and upgrade path detection), Case Study (e.g., industry, outcome metrics, used for matching relevant case studies), Sales Playbook (e.g., workflows, objections, positioning, used for selecting appropriate playbooks), Competitor Intel (e.g., strengths, win/loss themes, used for generating competitor cards), and Customer Patterns (e.g., pattern type, triggers, success rates, used for opportunity analysis). Each metadata model is designed to support filtered retrieval and agent-driven queries for sales and customer engagement scenarios.

nodes.title: 3.4 Product Relationship Graph
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.4 Product Relationship Graph

| Why This Is Our Proprietary Moat Foundry IQ does not know that Product A cross-sells with Product B, that Product C is an upgrade from Product D, or that Products E+F+G form a bundle. This domain-specific knowledge is what makes our recommendations intelligent rather than generic. The Product Relationship Graph is what we build; Foundry IQ cannot replace it. No competitor can replicate a tenant’s graph without their data and usage history. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 3.4.1 Graph Schema
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the schema for a product relationships graph table in a database. It outlines the structure of the table used to store relationships between products, including fields for product identifiers, relationship types (such as CROSS_SELL, UPGRADE_PATH, BUNDLE, REPLACES, REQUIRES, COMPETES_WITH), and whether the relationship is directional. The schema incorporates multiple confidence scores from different sources (statistical, LLM inference, usage data, and admin review), and defines a composite confidence score as a weighted combination of these. It also includes an evidence trail in JSON format to track the sources supporting each relationship, as well as timestamps for freshness tracking. Unique constraints and indexes are specified to optimize graph traversal and ensure data integrity.

nodes.title: 3.4.2 Relationship Types
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines various types of relationships that can exist between products, particularly in IT and insurance contexts. It presents a table describing each relationship type, its meaning, whether it is directional, and provides examples from both IT and insurance industries. The relationship types covered include: CROSS_SELL (complementary products), UPGRADE_PATH (higher-tier versions), BUNDLE (products sold together), REPLACES (new products superseding old ones), REQUIRES (dependency between products), and COMPETES_WITH (products from competitors). Each type is explained with clear examples to illustrate how these relationships manifest in different sectors.

nodes.title: 3.4.3 Four-Layer Graph Building Strategy
nodes.summary: This partial document describes a "Four-Layer Graph Building Strategy" for constructing product relationship graphs with minimal human effort. The process begins with automated analysis of purchase history to detect strong statistical relationships (cross-sell, upgrade, bundle, replace). It then leverages large language models (LLMs) to infer additional relationships from the product catalog, such as category complementarity and tiering, based on product descriptions and features. As the platform is used, it learns from real-world usage and sales outcomes to further refine and discover relationships. Finally, an optional human review layer allows administrators to confirm, edit, or reject suggested relationships, focusing only on likely connections rather than starting from scratch. The strategy emphasizes automation, confidence scoring, and efficient human oversight to build and maintain an accurate product relationship graph.

nodes.title: 3.4.4 Confidence Model
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Confidence Model" used to assign a composite confidence score to each graph edge. The score is calculated from four weighted sources: statistical data from purchase history (35%), LLM inference from catalog analysis (20%), usage metrics such as rep acceptance and deal close rates (30%), and explicit admin judgment (15%). Each source has a defined range, method of computation, and decay policy. The final score is computed using a weighted formula and stored as a generated column in PostgreSQL for efficient querying.

nodes.title: 3.4.5 Graph Traversal
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the implementation of graph traversal for product recommendation agents. It outlines a breadth-first search (BFS) algorithm used to explore product relationships starting from a customer’s current products, with configurable parameters such as relationship types, minimum confidence, and maximum traversal depth. The document details how different agents (e.g., Cross-Sell, Upsell, Full Solution, Account Overview, Background Preloader) use specific traversal settings tailored to their use cases. It also documents the architectural decision to use PostgreSQL with an indexed adjacency list for graph storage in the MVP, citing its adequacy for the expected data scale and simplicity, while reserving the option to migrate to a dedicated graph database like Neo4j if graph complexity grows significantly. The rationale emphasizes balancing performance, operational complexity, and scalability.

nodes.title: 3.5 Retrieval Layer — Multi-Source Query Orchestration
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 3.5 Retrieval Layer — Multi-Source Query Orchestration

When an agent needs knowledge, the Context Assembler (Module 1) calls the KB retrieval layer. This is not a single query — it is a parallel fan-out to multiple sources, with the sources and parameters determined by the agent’s manifest.

nodes.title: 3.5.1 Retrieval Flow
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Retrieval Flow" for a unified retrieval function that executes up to five parallel queries to gather relevant information for a conversation. The five queries include: (1) semantic retrieval using conversation context and customer profile, (2) product graph traversal to recommend products, (3) competitor store lookup for competitor analysis, (4) customer patterns query to analyze industry-specific behaviors, and (5) playbook index query to retrieve workflow-related guidance. Each query returns specialized results, and all are executed asynchronously to minimize latency, with overall retrieval time determined by the slowest query.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Which Agent Uses Which Sources
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines which data sources are utilized by various sales and support agents or plugins within a system. It presents a table mapping each agent/plugin (such as Cross-Sell Agent, Upsell Agent, Full Solution Agent, Competitor Card Plugin, Email Generator Plugin, KB Search Plugin, and Account Overview Plugin) to the specific information sources they use. The sources include Foundry IQ (case studies, tech specs, battle cards), Product Graph (different types of relationship edges), Competitor Store (competitor profiles and mentions), Customer Patterns (success, upgrade, win/loss patterns), and Playbooks (cross-sell, upsell, solution strategies). The table details how each agent leverages these sources to perform its function, highlighting the tailored use of data for cross-selling, upselling, competitive analysis, email generation, knowledge base search, and account overview tasks.

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Query Construction for Foundry IQ
nodes.summary: The partial document explains how retrieval queries for Foundry IQ are constructed from the current conversation state rather than using the user's raw message. It details the process of assembling the query by incorporating customer context (such as industry, segment, and existing product infrastructure), detected pain points, and agent-specific focus (like cross-sell, upsell, or full-solution options). The goal is to maximize the relevance of retrieved information by tailoring the query to the customer's profile, current products, discovered needs, and the agent's role.

nodes.title: 3.6 Cache Layer
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the caching strategy for different types of data in a system, focusing on how data volatility and access patterns influence cache configuration. It details what data is cached (such as product graph neighbors, product details, competitor profiles, and customer patterns), where it is cached (primarily Redis), the cache key patterns, time-to-live (TTL) settings, and specific triggers for cache invalidation. The document explains that cache invalidation is event-driven, with functions that clear relevant cache entries when underlying knowledge base content changes (e.g., product catalog updates, graph edge changes, competitor intel updates, or pattern recomputation). It also notes a key decision not to cache Foundry IQ results in Redis due to their highly contextual and dynamic nature, reserving caching for more static, structured data. The document includes code snippets illustrating the invalidation logic and emphasizes that Foundry IQ manages its own internal caching.

nodes.title: 3.7.1 How Different KB Components Update
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines how various Knowledge Base (KB) components are updated, detailing the triggers, mechanisms, and latency for each. It covers components such as Foundry IQ content, Product Catalog, multiple graph layers (statistical, LLM-inferred, usage, admin), Competitor Intel, and Customer Patterns. The document specifies who or what initiates updates (e.g., admin actions, platform signals, scheduled jobs), describes the update processes (e.g., auto-reindexing, batch computation, LLM analysis, real-time event-driven updates), and provides expected latency for each component, ranging from immediate to hours.

nodes.title: 3.7.2 Document Removal Flow
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the process and safeguards involved in removing a document from a system. It outlines a multi-step cascade that ensures all data and intelligence derived from the document are properly cleaned up. The steps include deleting the raw file from blob storage, updating the search index, removing related graph edges and competitor/customer intelligence contributions, performing a soft delete in the knowledge base catalog for audit purposes, and invalidating relevant caches. The document emphasizes the importance of tracking the source document ID for each piece of extracted intelligence, enabling precise removal of only the affected data while preserving intelligence sourced from other documents.

nodes.title: 3.7.3 Confidence Decay
nodes.summary: The partial document section discusses "Confidence Decay" in product graph relationships, outlining how different types of confidence (statistical, usage, admin, and LLM) are managed over time to prevent outdated relationships from influencing recommendations. Statistical confidence decays by 10% per month after six months without new co-purchases, while usage confidence decays by 15% per month after three months without rep acceptance. Admin confidence remains unchanged unless manually updated, and LLM confidence is recalculated with catalog updates. Decay is applied lazily during graph queries, adjusting confidence based on the time since the last update for each source.

nodes.title: 3.8 Nuances, Risks, and Design Decisions
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines key nuances, risks, and design decisions for implementing a knowledge management system using Foundry IQ. It highlights that only stable features should be used for the MVP, avoiding reliance on preview functionalities. The document discusses the cost implications of using LLMs for document classification, emphasizing the need for budgeting and rate limiting. It addresses the "cold start" problem for new tenants lacking transaction history, noting that initial recommendations will be less accurate but still functional. The potential for future cross-tenant pattern sharing is mentioned, with a caution about data governance. Finally, it stresses the importance of monitoring knowledge base quality through metrics like document categorization, staleness, unused content, and query coverage, all of which are essential for customer success and are to be tracked in an admin dashboard.

nodes.title: 3.9 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary: The partial document summarizes key technical decisions for a system architecture. It covers the choice to use Foundry IQ as a managed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) layer for unstructured document processing, streamlining engineering efforts and leveraging Microsoft’s enrichment and retrieval features. It details the decision to maintain a single Foundry IQ knowledge base per tenant, allowing agentic query routing across content types and simplifying source selection. The document explains storing the Product Graph in PostgreSQL as an adjacency list for the MVP, avoiding the complexity of Neo4j unless scaling demands change. It describes the use of an LLM-based Content Classifier to extract intelligence from documents and enrich multiple structured stores, enhancing system value with each document upload. Finally, it outlines caching strategies, emphasizing caching structured data in Redis for performance, but not caching Foundry IQ results due to their conversational context sensitivity.
